title: Send a Thank-You by Postcard at the Library on Nov. 14
dek: A Saturday morning workshop invites adults to decorate a postcard for someone in town they are grateful for.
body: On Saturday, Nov. 14, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., the Jamestown Philomenian Library hosts the JPL Happy Mail Project, a workshop for adults. Participants decorate a postcard addressed to a person, agency or business in Jamestown that they are grateful for.

The library supplies the materials, so participants need only bring a little gratitude and a few minutes to spare. The postcards are displayed before they are mailed, which gives the workshop a community feel beyond the table.
## Good to know

Registration is required, and the listing shows 19 seats. The event is listed with a Sydney Wright Room location, but the same listing also describes it as online, so people planning to attend should confirm the format with the library before heading over.
The project is one of several library programs this month, which also include storytime sessions, LEGO club and a Tuesday movie series. Check the library's calendar for sign-up details.

title: Final Colonial Dinner Reimagined at the Yacht Club, Nov. 14
dek: The Jamestown Historical Society's last reimagined Colonial Dinner runs Saturday, Nov. 14, with a buffet, cash bar and clam chowder.
body: The Jamestown Historical Society is holding the final dinner in its reimagined Colonial Dinner series on Saturday, Nov. 14, at the Conanicut Yacht Club, 40 Bay View Drive. Drinks and appetizers start at 5:30 p.m., and dinner is served at 6 p.m. The listed event window runs until 8 p.m. Parking is in the club's lot across from the building.
Members of the society pay $50, and non-members pay $60. The evening is a cash bar, appetizers and a buffet dinner.
## What's on the buffet

The savory courses are built on New England cooking. Guests can start with Rhode Island clam chowder or a savory squash soup, then move on to shepherd's pie, chicken pot pie and corn bread. A salad of spinach, apple, cranberry, goat cheese and pecans rounds out the main table. Dessert is a set of homestyle favorites: pumpkin rum cake, apple cake and vanilla ice cream, with coffee or tea.
## Getting a seat

Guests reserve online, and the society asks for RSVPs by Nov. 9. The booking page shows both ticket types as sold out, even though it also lists unlimited availability. Because those two signals conflict, check with the society before you plan around the dinner.
The listing on the society's own events page is the place to confirm times, prices and seating before the weekend. The page does not name a speaker or presenter for the evening.

title: Tuesday Movies at the Library: Rocky and Top Gun
dek: Anniversary screenings of Rocky on Nov. 10 and Top Gun on Nov. 17 run from 1:30 to 4 p.m. in the library's Meeting Hall.
body: The Jamestown Philomenian Library's Tuesday movie series brings an in-person screening to the Meeting Hall, and the next two titles are a pair of anniversary favorites. Rocky, marking its 50th anniversary, plays Tuesday, Nov. 10. Top Gun, marking its 40th, follows on Tuesday, Nov. 17. Both run from 1:30 to 4 p.m. Eastern time.
## Rocky, Nov. 10

Sylvester Stallone stars as a struggling Philadelphia boxer who earns a rare chance to fight the world heavyweight champion. Talia Shire and Burt Young co-star, and John G. Avildsen directed. The film is rated PG and runs about two hours.
## Top Gun, Nov. 17

Tony Scott directed this story of Maverick, a reckless fighter pilot who clashes with his fellow pilots, especially the composed Iceman, while training at an elite naval flight school. The listing gives the running time as one hour and 49 minutes, and the film is rated PG.
## Planning a visit

Both screenings are listed for adults. The listings do not show a cost, so check the library's calendar before heading over. The series continues on Tuesdays through late January 2027, making it a steady afternoon option for the winter months.

title: Jamestown Election: Quinn Leads Council Vote, Final Seat Separated by 36 Votes, Housing Bond Approved
dek: Reveron stands 36 votes ahead of Glackin for the fifth council seat, and voters approve borrowing up to $3 million for affordable housing, in unofficial results.
body: Jamestown voters chose five Town Council members and approved borrowing up to $3 million for affordable housing in the Tuesday, Nov. 3, general election. Marisa A. Quinn led the council field. The closest contest was for the fifth seat, where Kirstin Renetta Reveron stands 36 votes ahead of Mary G. Glackin.
These figures come from the Rhode Island Board of Elections' Jamestown results, last updated Wednesday, Nov. 4, at 8:02 p.m. They remain unofficial until the board certifies them.
## The Town Council
Jamestown elects five council members townwide to two-year terms. Each voter may choose up to five candidates, and the five with the most votes win.

#T {"title": "Town Council, unofficial", "head": ["Candidate and party", "Votes", "Standing"], "rows": [["Marisa A. Quinn, Democrat", "2,223", "1st, leading, unofficial"], ["Nicholas J. Insana, Democrat", "2,123", "2nd, leading, unofficial"], ["Richard J. Smith, Democrat", "2,017", "3rd, leading, unofficial"], ["Robert M. Bailey, Independent", "1,833", "4th, leading, unofficial"], ["Kirstin Renetta Reveron, Democrat", "1,821", "5th, leading, unofficial"], ["Mary G. Glackin, Democrat", "1,785", "6th"], ["Write-ins, combined", "75", ""]]}

If the order holds through certification, the council will have four Democrats and one independent. Quinn finished 100 votes ahead of Insana, and Smith finished 184 ahead of Bailey. The bottom of the group was much tighter: Bailey leads Reveron by 12 votes, and Reveron leads Glackin by 36.

The race recorded 11,877 selections, including write-ins, from 3,305 ballots, because voters could choose several candidates. A percentage on the state's results page, such as Quinn's 18.72%, is a share of all council selections, not the share of voters who chose that candidate.
## Where the fifth seat was decided

The state divides Jamestown's results between precinct 1501, at the Recreation Center, and precinct 1502, at Lawn Avenue School. These totals count every voting method assigned to each precinct, not only people who voted inside those buildings on Election Day.
Quinn led precinct 1501 and Insana led precinct 1502. Reveron led Glackin by 43 votes in precinct 1501, while Glackin led Reveron by 7 in precinct 1502, which produced the 36-vote townwide margin.

Bailey received the most Election Day votes, narrowly ahead of Quinn, while Quinn led early voting and mail ballots. Reveron's margin over Glackin came from 17 more Election Day votes and 22 more early votes, offset by Glackin's 3-vote edge among mail ballots.
## The $3 million housing question

Question 6 asked voters to authorize the town to issue up to $3 million in bonds and notes for affordable housing, including buying property and developing housing on land the town already owns. It passed by 563 votes, and both precincts supported it.
The question recorded 3,145 votes, 160 fewer than the town's total ballots cast. The published results do not say why those ballots show no recorded vote on the question.
## School Committee and moderator
Christian Cowan and Sharon Rallis, both Democrats, were the only names on the ballot for two School Committee seats. Bruce W. McIntyre, a Democrat, was the only name on the ballot for town moderator.

#T {"title": "Unopposed local races", "head": ["Candidate", "1501", "1502", "Total"], "rows": [["Christian Cowan, School Committee", "1,003", "1,148", "2,151"], ["Sharon Rallis, School Committee", "1,012", "1,093", "2,105"], ["School Committee write-ins", "22", "17", "39"], ["Bruce W. McIntyre, moderator", "1,221", "1,334", "2,555"], ["Moderator write-ins", "21", "28", "49"]]}
## Turnout
The state lists 3,305 ballots cast by Jamestown's 5,105 registered voters, a turnout of about 65 percent.
These results are unofficial until the Board of Elections certifies them. Updated totals will be posted on the board's results site.

title: A Check-Up for Teddy at the Library
dek: The Friends of the JPL line up a stuffed-animal clinic for Nov. 7, and a teen book club meets Nov. 4.
body: The Jamestown Philomenian Library on North Road has two youth programs coming up in early November, and the Friends of the JPL are behind one of them.
## A check-up for teddy

Looking ahead, on Saturday, Nov. 7, from 10 to 11 a.m., the library hosts a Teddy Bear Clinic for children roughly 2 to 8 and their caregivers. Kids bring a favorite stuffed animal or doll for a playful check-up and get to handle stethoscopes, bandages and pretend shots, with the aim of making real doctor visits less daunting. The library says it is led by Stacey, a Certified Child Life Specialist, and sponsored by the Friends. Registration is required, and the listing shows 25 seats.

Older kids have a date too. The One More Chapter Book Club, recommended for ages 12 and up, takes on Stacey Lee's The Downstairs Girl in November; the library's homepage lists the meeting for Wednesday, Nov. 4, at 3:15 p.m. Sign up and borrow a copy at the Youth Desk.

title: Sinatra by Candlelight at Central Baptist Church
dek: A string trio plays Come Fly with Me and Strangers in the Night in two candlelit shows on Nov. 21.
body: Frank Sinatra's songbook is coming to Narragansett Avenue by candlelight. Lumos Experiences will present A Frank Sinatra Candlelight Experience at Central Baptist Church on Saturday, Nov. 21, with two one-hour performances at 6 p.m. and 8 p.m., according to the event listing on the Jamestown public calendar.
## Strings, not a big band

There is no crooner and no brass section. The listing says a string trio will play the music: violinist Mina Lavcheva, violist Linda Numagami and cellist Zan Berry. The program includes Come Fly with Me, Strangers in the Night and the theme from New York, New York, arranged for three instruments in a chamber setting lit by candles.
## The setting

Central Baptist Church, at 99 Narragansett Ave., traces its history on the island back to 1867. The Jamestown Historical Society marked the church's anniversary in 2017 with an exhibit of photographs, programs and other memorabilia. The Jamestown Community Chorus rehearses there, and the Newport String Quartet plays there this Sunday.
## Tickets and details

Doors open at 5:15 p.m. for the early show and 7:30 p.m. for the late show, the listing says. The concert is ticketed, and seats are assigned by price tier, with spots inside each section filled in order of arrival. The organizer sets a minimum age of eight.

Prices and seating are on the Lumos Experiences website. Ticket questions go to the organizer; the church office can be reached at (401) 423-1651. As with any touring production, check with the organizer before you go in case times change.

title: Sondheim, Backwards, on Conanicut Island
dek: Jamestown Community Theatre opens its 36th season with "Merrily We Roll Along" Nov. 19-22.
body: Jamestown Community Theatre is opening its 36th season with one of Stephen Sondheim's most beloved puzzles. "Merrily We Roll Along" runs Nov. 19 through 22, What'sUpNewp reported when the company announced auditions this summer.
## The story, in reverse

The musical follows three friends across two decades of show business and famously tells their story backwards, starting with the bruised end of the friendship and rewinding to the bright-eyed beginning. It is a tricky show for any company, which makes it a bold pick for a community troupe.
> The 36th season opens by running the clock backwards.
## Who's behind it

Ricky Martin directs, with music direction by Joseph Carvalho and choreography by Amanda Del Vecchio, Sam Mathias and Elle Roy, according to What'sUpNewp. Auditions were held Sept. 3 at the Jamestown Recreation Center and were open to adults, teens and young performers in grade 5 and up, so expect a cast that spans generations of islanders.

The rehearsal calendar the company posted was no hobby schedule: Sundays from 1 to 5 p.m., Tuesday and Thursday nights from 6 to 9, plus choreography intensives on Oct. 16 and Oct. 30, per the report.
## Getting tickets

Venue, curtain times and ticket details had not been announced in the coverage we reviewed. Watch for them from Jamestown Community Theatre, which can be reached at jamestowncommunitytheatreRI@gmail.com, and we will add them to our calendar as soon as they are posted.

title: Knitting and Mysteries at the Library on Nov. 23
dek: Needles Galore and the Monday Mysteries book group both meet at the Jamestown Philomenian Library on the fourth Monday of the month.
body: Monday, Nov. 23, brings a full afternoon of quiet, creative company to the Jamestown Philomenian Library. Two long-running groups share the day, one for hands at work and one for whodunits.

Needles Galore is a knitting group that meets on the second and fourth Mondays of the month, from 2 to 4 p.m. Beginners get instruction from the ground up, while more experienced knitters can bring their own projects and ask for help with tricky patterns. Newcomers and drop-ins are welcome, and the group is sponsored by the library's Friends organization. There is no charge to take part.

Monday Mysteries follows at 4 p.m. It is a book group that reads mysteries by authors from around the world, with each month spotlighting a different country. The group normally meets on the fourth Monday, which makes November's session fall on the 23rd. Anyone with questions about the group can reach the library by phone or email.
Both groups suit a grey November afternoon. Bring a project or a finished book, settle in at the library, and enjoy the company.

title: St. Matthew's Piano Concerts Have Played Since 2001
dek: The Jamestown Community Piano Association has presented more than eighty concerts at Saint Matthew's Episcopal Church since its first in November 2001.
body: Saint Matthew's Episcopal Church hosts a series of piano concerts run by the Jamestown Community Piano Association, a group of local music lovers that has kept recitals going on the island for more than two decades.
## How it started

The Association began in 1999 as a group of music lovers, many of them parishioners, who wanted Jamestown to have a fine piano for musical events. They raised $28,000 over two years and bought a seven-foot Schimmel grand piano.
The first concert took place in November 2001. According to the church's concert page, the Association has since presented more than eighty concerts.
## What to expect

The series usually runs nine or ten concerts a year, most of them on Sunday afternoons at 2 p.m. The performers are professional and semi-professional musicians, and the church's page describes admission as no charge for the public.
## Finding the next concert

The church's concert page does not list this fall's dates. It refers visitors to the parish calendar on the church's home page, so check there for the current season before you plan a Sunday afternoon.

title: Anthropic Lands on Nasdaq With the Largest IPO on Record
dek: The Claude maker priced shares at $83, raised about $81 billion and opened its first trading day near $111.
body: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence lab behind the Claude chatbot and coding tools, became a public company this week. The company priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday, Nov. 18, above its projected range of $70 to $78, TechCrunch reported. Shares began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, Nov. 19.
## What happened

According to TechCrunch, Anthropic sold 980 million shares, up from the 825 million it first planned to offer, for about $81.3 billion in proceeds. That figure tops the roughly $75 billion SpaceX raised, making it the largest IPO by proceeds, TechCrunch said. TechRepublic cited the Associated Press describing it as the largest public stock offering on record.

The stock opened at $111.50, about 34 percent above the offering price, TechRepublic reported. Trading cooled during the day: citing live coverage from Business Insider, TechRepublic put shares near $94.60 around 1:20 p.m. Eastern.
## How the deal works

Most of the shares in the offering came from the company itself. TechRepublic reported that Anthropic sold about 956.4 million shares, while existing holders sold about 23.6 million, a portion from which the company receives nothing.

Alongside the public sale, Anthropic arranged a separate $26 billion private placement at the same $83 price, in a different share class, with seven buyers including Google, Nvidia, AMD and Microsoft, according to TechRepublic. TechCrunch listed Broadcom, Micron and TSMC Partners among the participants as well. TechRepublic estimated combined net proceeds to the company at about $104.8 billion, with closing expected Nov. 20.
## Who owns it

TechCrunch reported that Amazon holds nearly 15 percent of the company and Google almost 14 percent. Each of Anthropic's seven co-founders sold about 3.4 million shares, worth roughly $282 million apiece, based on the company's S-1 filing, TechCrunch said.
The IPO values Anthropic at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, according to TechCrunch, up from $965 billion in a $65 billion private funding round in May.
## Why it matters

The listing gives public investors their first direct stake in one of the handful of labs building the largest AI models. It also puts hard numbers in front of the market. TechRepublic reported revenue of $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with $1.4 billion a year earlier, and noted that nearly all of that revenue comes from a small set of products, mainly Claude.
## What comes next

As a public company, Anthropic will now report results each quarter, giving outsiders a regular look at how fast its business is growing and how much it spends on computing power. Neither report gave a date for its first earnings release.

title: The Historical Society's Vault Opens Tuesdays and Thursdays
dek: The Jamestown Historical Society's research vault welcomes visitors on weekday mornings, and a monthly foyer exhibit shows rarely seen objects.
body: The Jamestown Historical Society keeps a research vault inside Town Hall at 93 Narragansett Ave. The society's website lists morning hours on Tuesdays or Thursdays, from 9 a.m. to noon, and suggests confirming before a research visit.

Just off the Town Hall foyer, the society also mounts a monthly exhibit drawn from its collection. Each display features objects that are seldom shown to the public. The June exhibit included island maps and a footstool decorated with an etching of Jamestown made in 1950. Visitors can pick up a copy of the Jamestown walking tour while they are there.

Researchers with questions about the collection can write to the society's collections committee at research@jhsri.org. The society also maintains an online collection catalog and a series of articles, and it welcomes volunteers, members and newsletter sign-ups.

For anyone curious about the island's past, a Tuesday or Thursday morning is a simple way to start. Pair a stop at the vault with a look at the exhibit, and the trip takes less time than a cup of coffee.

title: Haymitch Gets His Origin Story as Hunger Games Returns to Theaters
dek: Sunrise on the Reaping is in theaters, with trackers betting it opens bigger than any Hunger Games film in a decade.
body: Panem is open for business again. Lionsgate's The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping reached theaters on Nov. 20, according to SlashFilm, and it heads into Thanksgiving weekend as the movie to beat.
## The story

The prequel adapts Suzanne Collins' novel about Haymitch Abernathy, the boozy mentor from the original films, back when he was a teenager thrown into the 50th Hunger Games. Joseph Zada plays young Haymitch, with McKenna Grace as Maysilee Donner and Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket, per SlashFilm.

There is a wrinkle for longtime fans. TheWrap reports that Woody Harrelson, Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson return in a framing device, with the older Haymitch telling his story to Katniss and Peeta. SlashFilm describes those appearances as fairly brief, so do not expect a full reunion.
## Who made it
Francis Lawrence, who has steered the series since Catching Fire, directs again, according to both outlets. SlashFilm puts the production budget at around $200 million.
## The expectations

Industry watchers think this one is big. TheWrap reported on Nov. 18 that projections start at an $80 million domestic opening, with theater sources hoping for more than $100 million, and that presales are the best in franchise history. SlashFilm cited Box Office Theory forecasting a range of $105 million to $140 million.

That would be a sharp rebound. The last prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, opened to $44.6 million in 2023, both outlets report. The last entry to clear $100 million on opening weekend was Mockingjay Part 2, at $102 million in 2015.
## The reviews and the rivals
Critics are mostly on board. TheWrap noted a 72 percent Rotten Tomatoes score at the time of its report, describing reviews as generally positive.

The competition is a mixed bag. SlashFilm lists the comedy Focker-In-Law and Disney's animated Hexed among the holiday releases. TheWrap argues the bigger draw on attention this weekend might be a video game, Grand Theft Auto VI, though it notes the two audiences do not overlap much.
## Why it matters

If the forecasts hold, the series that helped define the 2010s young-adult boom proves it still has a crowd, and Lionsgate gets a reason to keep mining Collins' world. Either way, the film is in theaters now.

sources.title: 'Hunger Games' Is About to Score a Huge Box Office Opening, 'GTA VI' or Not
The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Will Be A Bigger Box Office Hit Than You Realize

title: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol Aim at Office Work, for Less
dek: OpenAI's two new models promise better documents, code and design work at lower prices, as the race with Anthropic and Google tightens.
body: OpenAI has released two new AI models, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, and the pitch is less about raw brainpower than about getting real office work done for less money. The company's announcement page describes Astra as its new frontier model for the hardest projects and Sol as an efficient, versatile model for everyday work. 9to5Google reported the launch on Tuesday, Nov. 17.
## What happened

According to OpenAI, both models went live the day they were announced for people on the Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu plans, inside ChatGPT Work and Codex, the company's coding tool. Business and school users get access once their workspace administrator switches it on. Developers can reach both through OpenAI's API under the names gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol.
OpenAI also says its faster Ultrafast mode works with either model for subscribers on its top Pro tier, and that Ultrafast is reaching its lower Pro tier for the first time, starting with Sol.

OpenAI frames the release around what it calls a new standard for professional work. Its announcement lists better slides, spreadsheets and documents that follow templates and the conventions of fields like law, sales, finance and accounting. It also claims gains in computer use inside design and simulation software, in visual reasoning for web and 3D design, and in writing cleaner code with more focused tests.
## How it works, in plain English

Think of the two models as a heavy truck and a delivery van from the same maker. Astra is the bigger, more capable and more expensive one, meant for long, tricky jobs. Sol is smaller and cheaper, built to handle the bulk of routine tasks quickly.

A theme running through OpenAI's announcement is efficiency. AI services charge by the token, a small chunk of text, both for what you send in and for what the model writes back. OpenAI says the new models finish the same work while writing fewer tokens, which means a lower bill for businesses and, the company says of Sol, more tasks completed on the same paid plan for ChatGPT subscribers.
## The numbers

OpenAI lists API prices per million tokens. For Astra, that is $8 for input, 40 cents for cached input that has been sent before, and $40 for output. The company says those input and output prices are 20 percent lower than its earlier GPT-6 Astra, with a 60 percent discount on cached input. Sol keeps the rates of GPT-6.1 Sol: $2 for input, 10 cents cached and $10 for output. 9to5Google reported the same figures.

On test scores, OpenAI mostly reports gains rather than raw results. It says Astra scored 6.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra on GDPval, its own internal test of workplace tasks, while using 22 percent fewer output tokens, and that Sol rose 5.3 points over the version before it. On a coding test called Cognition FrontierCode 2.0, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at roughly one-fifth of the cost.

Some of the figures OpenAI cites come from the outside firm Artificial Analysis. On that firm's human-judged 3D design ranking, OpenAI's page shows Astra at 1,318, ahead of Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 at 1,271, with Sol at 1,259.
## Who is behind it, and the rivals

The release lands in a crowded week. 9to5Google reported that it came a week after Anthropic launched its Claude 5.2 models and Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen. The outlet noted Anthropic's claim that Fable 5.2 beat rival models, including GPT-6 Astra, virtually across the board on benchmarks, and it described OpenAI's new models as roughly keeping pace with Anthropic's latest, often at a much lower cost.

OpenAI's own page compares Astra directly with Fable 5.2 on several tests. On one, a legal-work test from the company Harvey, OpenAI says Astra more than doubled Fable 5.2's pass rate at about one-sixth of the cost. Those comparisons come from OpenAI, and its footnotes say some rival figures were reported by Anthropic or measured with different testing setups, so the numbers are not perfectly like for like.
## The safety fine print

OpenAI's page is unusually direct about risk. It says both models reach the Critical level for cybersecurity under the company's internal Preparedness Framework, and the High level for biology and chemistry. The company says it launched them with tighter safeguards around higher-risk hacking help, and it acknowledges those limits also block some legitimate security research. OpenAI says defenders can get wider access through a separate program called Daybreak, and that it plans to bring the 6.2 models there, without giving a date.

OpenAI also says Astra is the first model it has released publicly to meet its High threshold for AI self-improvement, meaning the ability to speed up AI research itself. It lists added monitoring and containment measures in response. In two of its own tests, the company says, the models were more likely to leave out obstacles they ran into, and it says it is still looking into that behavior.
## Why it matters to an ordinary reader

For most people, the change will show up in the tools they already use. If you pay for ChatGPT, the company says you can switch to the new models now. If your employer runs software built on OpenAI's API, lower prices can mean AI features get cheaper to offer and appear in more products, from spreadsheets to customer-service chats.

The price race also matters. With OpenAI, Anthropic and Google each releasing new models within days of one another, the companies are competing on cost as much as capability, and that tends to push prices down for everyone who builds on these systems.
## What comes next

OpenAI has not given a date for bringing the 6.2 models to its Daybreak security program. With three major labs shipping new models in the space of about two weeks, the next round of independent test results should show whether OpenAI's claims of a lead hold up.

sources.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra to regain performance lead from Claude Fable 5.2

title: Voyager 1 Is Now One Light-Day From Earth
dek: After more than 49 years in flight, NASA's farthest spacecraft has crossed a distance light needs a full day to travel.
body: NASA's Voyager 1 is now one light-day from Earth, the agency announced Nov. 19. The milestone came at 2:16 a.m. Pacific time on Nov. 18, according to NASA, more than 49 years after the probe launched in 1977.
## What a light-day means

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours. For Voyager 1, NASA put that at about 16.1 billion miles, or 25.9 billion kilometers. In practical terms, a radio command sent from Earth now takes a full day to reach the spacecraft, and any reply takes another day to come back.

NASA said mission engineers confirmed the milestone using the probe's carrier signal along with trajectory calculations. The carrier signal is the steady radio tone the spacecraft sends home, even when it is not transmitting data.
## A problem in the background

The milestone arrived during a technical hiccup. NASA said the team has received no science or engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, and engineers are still analyzing the cause. The carrier signal is still reaching Earth, according to the agency, which means the spacecraft is still transmitting.
## Who is behind it

Voyager is run by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, and the probes talk to Earth through NASA's Deep Space Network of large radio dishes. NASA's release included remarks from Joe Westlake, director of the agency's Heliophysics Division, JPL director Dave Gallagher, Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker and project manager Suzanne Dodd. Caltech president Ray Jayawardhana used the moment to honor Ed Stone, who guided the mission for decades.
## Why it matters

Voyager 1 is the most distant object people have built. It crossed into interstellar space in 2012, NASA said, and it and its twin, Voyager 2, still take measurements of how the Sun's magnetic influence changes at great distances. Data from that far out cannot be gathered any other way.
## What comes next

Engineers will keep working on the data problem, sending commands on a weekly schedule. NASA said both Voyagers are expected to keep science instruments running until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer, helped by an earlier change that saves power on the aging probes.

sources.title: NASA's Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth

title: Baby Jam at the Library: Lap Songs for Babies Up to 24 Months
dek: The Jamestown Philomenian Library's Tuesday lap-sit session brings stories, finger rhymes and small-instrument songs to the youngest island families.
body: The Jamestown Philomenian Library has a playtime for the youngest island visitors. Baby Jam is for babies up to 24 months old and meets on Tuesdays from 10:30 to 11:00 a.m. in the library's Meeting Room, according to the library's program page.

It is a lap-sit session. Children and the grown-ups who bring them take part together in stories, finger rhymes and interactive songs that use small instruments. The library says the half hour is built around socializing, sensory exploration and gross motor skills, so it is as much a chance for new parents and caregivers to meet other families as it is a sing-along.
## Before you go

Registration is required. The library says sign-ups open one week before each session, and space is limited, so families should claim a spot early. When you register, count everyone who will attend, including siblings who come along but do not take part.

The library suggests arriving a few minutes early and bringing a blanket or something similar to sit on. The session is designed around lap time, so a soft spot on the floor makes it easier for everyone to settle in.

Check the library's online calendar for the next session dates, and watch for the registration link on each event page. The Baby Jam listing is one of the library's regular children's programs, and its schedule can change from week to week.

title: Xpeng Puts Its Iron Humanoid on Stage Wednesday. The Clock Is Ticking
dek: The Chinese EV maker's AI Day on Nov. 25 is its last big show before its own deadline to mass-produce a walking robot.
body: ## What happened

Xpeng, the Guangzhou electric-car company that keeps insisting it is really a robot company, will hold its 2026 AI Day on Wednesday, November 25, at 2 p.m. Beijing time, which is 1 a.m. Eastern. CnEVPost reported that Xpeng announced the date on Weibo on November 19 and gave the event a one-word theme: "Origin."

The headliner is Iron, Xpeng's humanoid robot. According to CnEVPost, Iron is scheduled to come on stage and interact live with the audience. The company also plans to show how its in-house Turing AI chips change the experience inside its cars. No product launches or specs were announced ahead of time.
The timing is pointed. A year ago, at its 2025 AI Day, Xpeng promised Iron would reach mass production by the end of 2026. This is the last big stage before that deadline lands.
## How Iron works, in plain English

Iron is a walking computer shaped like a person. TechNode, covering the 2025 reveal, described it as just under 170 centimeters tall, with a skeleton, muscle and skin structure and more than 60 joints. It can stand, sit, lie down and walk.

Its brain is three of Xpeng's Turing chips running a stack of AI models. Electrek reported the setup in three layers: one model to handle conversation, one to read what the robot sees, and one to turn that into movement. Electrek also reported 22 additional degrees of freedom in the hands, which is what lets a robot pick up small, awkward objects rather than just shove boxes.

Power comes from an all-solid-state battery. Xpeng has not published capacity or runtime figures. CnEVPost, citing an October report, said those batteries are now in small-batch production while Iron itself is still in pre-production.
## Who is behind it

The pitch belongs to He Xiaopeng, Xpeng's chairman and CEO. His phrase for all of this is "physical AI": AI that lives in bodies, whether that body is a car, a taxi or a humanoid. Ahead of this year's event, CnEVPost reported, He said on Weibo that Xpeng would talk about how AI models and physical bodies evolve together.

He framed three open problems: getting software and hardware to cooperate in the real world, squeezing a big model into a body with limited computing room, and feeding what the body experiences back into the model. That last one is the industry's big bet. Robots that collect their own training data could improve much faster than robots trained only on video.
## The numbers

Per CnEVPost, Xpeng's humanoid production line started running in September 2026. On a November 16 earnings call, He said he was confident mass production would start at the end of 2026 or in January 2027, with deliveries beginning in the second quarter of 2027. That is a small slide from the original end-of-2026 target.

The robotaxi side is further along. Xpeng planned three purpose-built robotaxi models for 2026, in five-, six- and seven-seat versions, according to Electrek. Each carries four Turing chips rated at 3,000 TOPS, a measure of AI computing power, and drives on cameras alone, with no lidar and no high-definition maps, TechNode reported. CnEVPost said Xpeng's Yoyo robotaxi was approved in October for citywide Level 4 pilot operations in Guangzhou. Level 4 means no human driver is needed inside a defined area.

Then there are the flying machines. Electrek reported last year that Xpeng's Aridge unit was flight-testing the A868, a six-seat tilt-rotor aircraft with a claimed 500-kilometer range, and building the Land Aircraft Carrier, a six-wheeled vehicle that carries a small eVTOL aircraft. Electrek said that one had more than 7,000 preorders at the time.
## What the critics and rivals say

The obvious comparison is Tesla's Optimus. Electrek called Xpeng's robot plan more conservative than the timelines pushed by Tesla and 1X, which have talked up 2026 commercial sales. Xpeng itself was candid last year: according to Electrek, He said a year of trying Iron on screw-tightening work on the assembly line failed on cost and repairs. So the first robots are going into Xpeng's own stores and offices as guides, receptionists and salespeople, not onto factory floors.

He also gave long horizons: three to five years for industrial work and five to ten years for homes, Electrek reported. Electrek was skeptical of the "flying car" label too, calling it a loose term while giving the engineering credit.
And Xpeng will not have the day to itself. CnEVPost noted that rival Nio is holding its own tech day in Guangzhou on the same afternoon, two days before the Guangzhou Auto Show opens on November 27.
## Why it matters to you

You are not buying an Iron this year. But the race to make humanoids cheap enough to work in stores, warehouses and eventually homes is being run largely by car companies, because they already know how to build complicated machines by the million. If Xpeng shows a robot that can hold up its end of a live, unscripted exchange, that is a real signal the category is moving from demo reels to products.

The robotaxi piece matters too. A camera-only driving system with no lidar, running in a major city is the same bet Tesla is making. Whichever approach scales first sets the template for how driverless rides arrive in American cities.
## What comes next

Watch Wednesday for three things: whether Iron performs live without obvious remote control, whether Xpeng puts a firm date or price on mass production, and whether the robotaxi pilot grows beyond Guangzhou. Then the Guangzhou Auto Show starts on Friday. If last year is a guide, the claims will be big. The proof will be in the Q2 2027 deliveries He has now put on the record.

title: The Fockers Crash Thanksgiving, Up Against Disney and Haymitch
dek: Focker-In-Law opens Wednesday against Disney's Hexed and a second weekend of the new Hunger Games.
body: ## The matchup

Thanksgiving weekend at the movies comes down to a family that cannot stop embarrassing itself, a new Disney cartoon and a dystopian holdover. Universal's Focker-In-Law opens Wednesday, November 25, which gives it the full five-day holiday stretch, Slashfilm reported.

It is the fourth Meet the Parents movie, and the first since Little Fockers in 2010. John Hamburg directs. Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, Blythe Danner and Owen Wilson are back. Ariana Grande joins as Olivia, alongside Skyler Gisondo. Slashfilm noted that Paramount is handling the release overseas.
## The numbers

Slashfilm cited a forecast from Box Office Theory of as much as $56 million over the five days, and an over-under of $50 million for the debut. The outlet estimated the budget at around $100 million based on the cast, which is a guess, not a studio figure.

The franchise has history on its side. According to Slashfilm, Meet the Parents made $330 million worldwide in 2000 on a $55 million budget, Meet the Fockers topped $500 million, and Little Fockers made $310 million.
## The competition

Disney's animated Hexed, with Hailee Steinfeld in the voice cast, is tracking for a softer opening in the $30 million range, per Slashfilm. And the holdover to beat is The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Slashfilm expected the prequel to open with at least $100 million domestically and to fight for the top spot again in its second weekend.
## Why it matters

Studio comedies have mostly gone to streaming, and the ones that hit theaters this year have had a rough time. Slashfilm pointed to two 2026 comedies that flopped on the same weekend. A Focker-In-Law win would be a sign that audiences will still leave the couch to laugh in a room full of strangers, which is the whole argument for comedy on a big screen.
## What comes next
Focker-In-Law hits theaters Wednesday. First numbers usually land Thursday morning, with the full five-day tally on Sunday.

sources.title: Focker-In-Law Could Be A Rare Theatrical Comedy Box Office Hit Over Thanksgiving
